# Place, Route, Timing, and Programming with nextpnr

[]{#ref-nextpnr .reference-destination}

[]{#ref-bitstream .reference-destination}

## Concepts

[]{#ref-nextpnr-timing-concepts .reference-destination}

Yosys establishes which FPGA primitives implement the design. Physical implementation decides where they go, which programmable wires connect them and whether signals can arrive within the available clock period. For Xilinx 7-series devices, the open stack combines `nextpnr-xilinx` with Project X-Ray device data. nextpnr is timing-driven free and open-source place-and-route software; XC7 support is marked experimental, so each bitstream needs explicit report review and hardware validation [@nextpnrRepository].

The implementation has a causal chain:

```text
JSON netlist + XDC constraints
             |
       pack / place / route
             |
 nextpnr report + routed JSON + FASM features
             |
     fasm2frames -> frame data
             |
   xc7frames2bit -> configuration bitstream
             |
 openFPGALoader -> volatile SRAM or nonvolatile flash
```

**Packing** groups logical cells into legal FPGA sites; **placement** chooses sites; **routing** selects programmable interconnect; and **static timing analysis (STA)** evaluates delays in the resulting implementation. These are not separate decorations. A valid location may introduce a long route; a change in placement can alter both slack and congestion.

### Constraints are part of the design

An XDC file connects the logical top-level ports to the Nexys Video board and states the electrical/timing assumptions. A typical fragment from the open Wally constraints is:

```tcl
set_property -dict {PACKAGE_PIN R4 IOSTANDARD LVCMOS33} \
  [get_ports default_100mhz_clk]
set_property -dict {PACKAGE_PIN G4 IOSTANDARD LVCMOS15} \
  [get_ports resetn]
set_property -dict {PACKAGE_PIN AA19 IOSTANDARD LVCMOS33} \
  [get_ports UARTSout]
```

Every signal must use the voltage standard of its bank and connected peripheral. A correct port name with the wrong IO standard can produce a board that fails electrically, while an unconstrained port makes the physical result non-reproducible. Keep the XDC together with the board wrapper and review it when either changes.

Timing constraints state facts that pins do not: input clock frequency, generated clocks, external IO requirements and the rare intentional exceptions. The board oscillator is 100 MHz, but the open Nexys Video Wally configuration targets a 40 MHz system clock produced as part of its open design. The 40 MHz number is the requirement for the routing run, and every derived domain still has to be understood separately.

### What timing closure means

For a same-clock register-to-register path, the available time is the period after clock uncertainty, skew and setup requirement. The data path includes clock-to-Q delay, LUT/carry logic and physical routing. Slack is required time minus arrival time.

| Result | Interpretation | Action |
|---|---|---|
| Positive worst slack | Constrained checked paths meet the stated target | Review coverage and hold checks |
| Negative setup slack | A path is too slow for the requested period | Change microarchitecture, constraints or target frequency |
| Unconstrained clock/path | The tool cannot establish the required relationship | Add/correct constraints before trusting the build |
| Passed at a lower frequency | Functional configuration may be useful for bring-up | Do not claim the higher target is closed |

Timing closure shows that the paths meet their constraints, and functional correctness, CDC safety and DDR calibration are separate questions. In the other direction, an RTL simulation with correct behavior says nothing about delay through an actual FPGA. A trustworthy result needs both forms of evidence.

### Routed FPGA verification and timing closure

Use @sec-verification-methodology to review clocks, I/O constraints, routed resources and all applicable timing paths. Check setup and hold, generated clocks, unconstrained endpoints and justified exceptions. Tie the timing report to the actual routed design and emitted bitstream. A completed place-and-route command only means the tool finished, and the report says whether the selected clock target was met. Configuration changes, debug instrumentation and routing seeds can change results, so record their identities and repeat the affected checks instead of reusing an old frequency claim.


## Implementation

**Recipe status: adaptation template.** Provide the pinned XC7 tools/database, generated netlist, constraints and firmware described by the selected Wally snapshot. Routing and bitstream commands require those external inputs, and their success is a build result that says nothing yet about board operation. Timing-budget modifications are exercises with their own reports.


### nextpnr-xilinx and Project X-Ray

`nextpnr-xilinx` reads the Yosys JSON netlist, XDC constraints and a chip database for the FPGA die. Project X-Ray supplies the reverse-engineered database and bitstream tooling for Xilinx 7-series [@projectXray]. The tool produces three important implementation artifacts:

| File | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `nexysvideo-routed.json` | Netlist after packing, placement and routing |
| `nexysvideo-report.json` | Resource, placement and timing-report data |
| `nexysvideo.fasm` | Human-readable FPGA assembly features |

FASM is not the hardware configuration itself. It records enabled FPGA features in a textual form. `fasm2frames` converts those features into frame data using the Project X-Ray database, and `xc7frames2bit` serializes frame data into the `.bit` configuration file for the exact part.

@fig-xilinx-flow follows the files from the Yosys netlist to a configured board.

![From the Yosys netlist to a configured FPGA in the open Xilinx 7-series flow. nextpnr-xilinx writes the routed netlist, a report and the FASM file; fasm2frames and xc7frames2bit turn the FASM features into the bitstream that a programmer loads. The figure shows the file flow and not the run time of any step.](../../figures/nextpnr-xilinx-to-bitstream.svg){#fig-xilinx-flow width=100% fig-alt="Inputs to nextpnr-xilinx, its three output files and the path from FASM to a programmed board"}

The full CVW command is deliberately short because the generated artifacts carry the detail:

```sh
nextpnr-xilinx \
  --chipdb "$NEXTPNR_XILINX_CHIPDB_XC7A200T" \
  --xdc opensource-nexysvideo/constraints.xdc \
  --json opensource-nexysvideo/nexysvideo.json \
  --top fpgaOpenSource \
  --freq 40 \
  --write opensource-nexysvideo/nexysvideo-routed.json \
  --report opensource-nexysvideo/nexysvideo-report.json \
  --fasm opensource-nexysvideo/nexysvideo.fasm
```

`--freq 40` supplies the 40 MHz implementation target. It must agree with the actual synchronous design and the declared clocks. It is not a way to cover for a missing generated-clock or external-interface constraint. The `--top` value must be the same one Yosys synthesized.

### Device database and part identity

The Nexys Video board uses the `xc7a200tsbg484-1` part. The branch selects the `xc7a200t` chip database and the complete part string for frame conversion. Those names are not interchangeable:

```sh
fasm2frames --db-root "$XRAY_DATABASE_DIR" \
  --part xc7a200tsbg484-1 \
  opensource-nexysvideo/nexysvideo.fasm \
  opensource-nexysvideo/nexysvideo.frames

xc7frames2bit \
  --part_file "$XRAY_DATABASE_DIR/xc7a200tsbg484-1/part.yaml" \
  --part_name xc7a200tsbg484-1 \
  --frm_file opensource-nexysvideo/nexysvideo.frames \
  --output_file opensource-nexysvideo/nexysvideo.bit
```

Always retain the database revision. A bitstream built for a different package, speed grade or device is a risk to the board and should never be loaded. Let scripts derive values from one board definition rather than duplicating part strings across files.

### Reading the report

Inspect the nextpnr terminal output and the JSON report after every implementation. At minimum answer these questions:

1. Did all intended top-level ports receive locations and IO standards?
2. Does utilization leave adequate LUT, flip-flop, BRAM, DSP, IO and clocking headroom?
3. Which clock domains were timed and which were not?
4. What is the worst setup slack and its launch/capture endpoints?
5. Are there warnings about routing, pack failures, unavailable resources or ignored constraints?
6. Does the achieved maximum frequency exceed the requested frequency with enough margin for the experiment?

The CVW Nexys Video implementation reports the principal `HCLK`, `clk100` and IDELAY-related paths. Its documented current limitation is important: the DDR PHY `sys4x` domain is not fully constrained in this open flow, even though the complete design creates a bitstream. This means the result is a useful reproducible bring-up platform, not timing closure for a production DDR3 subsystem [@cvwOpenSourceFpga].

### Clock, reset and CDC review

The open configuration runs Wally and the LiteDRAM controller in one shared system clock domain. The arrangement avoids an AHB-to-Wishbone CDC bridge: a bus transfer carries address, write data, byte enables and response semantics, so a two-flop synchronizer would be invalid. Wally remains in reset until the DDR initialization path reports successful completion.

This is a good integration decision for a first hardware prototype. It does not remove the need to analyze asynchronous inputs, the JTAG/UART boundaries, resets and generated clocks. In particular:

- Synchronize a pushbutton/reset release and any asynchronous peripheral input.
- State how the board oscillator reaches a global buffer and clock primitive.
- Use clock enables for slow functions, and keep LUT-gated clocks out of the design.
- Describe every clock domain and its relationship to every other domain.
- Put exceptions next to the CDC protocol that justifies them; a false path is never the answer to an ordinary failing register path.

The clocking and timing foundations chapter explains the relevant setup/hold and CDC principles in detail.

### From FASM to `.bit`

Project X-Ray makes the open bitstream step explicit. This gives valuable auditability: a routed JSON and FASM file are inspectable evidence of the placed/routed configuration that produced the bitstream. It also exposes a practical boundary: coverage and tool maturity differ among FPGA families and primitives. Lock tool/database versions for any published result.

Once the commands complete, check that the expected files exist and record checksums:

```sh
sha256sum opensource-nexysvideo/nexysvideo.json \
          opensource-nexysvideo/nexysvideo-report.json \
          opensource-nexysvideo/nexysvideo.fasm \
          opensource-nexysvideo/nexysvideo.bit
```

The `.bit` is a configuration image, not a software executable. It can include initialized BRAM contents, so its checksum changes when firmware changes even if the processor RTL does not.

### Programming the Nexys Video physically

Connect the Nexys Video board through its USB-JTAG connection, apply stable board power and identify the programmer before loading any image. `openFPGALoader` supports volatile SRAM configuration and configuration-flash programming; list board targets and inspect the installed help because option spelling can change between releases [@openFPGALoader].

Start with volatile configuration. It disappears after power cycling, which makes it safer during bring-up:

```sh
openFPGALoader --list-boards
openFPGALoader --board nexys_video \
  opensource-nexysvideo/nexysvideo.bit
```

If the installed board definition uses a different spelling, use the result of `--list-boards`; a similar Nexys model is not a safe substitute. Confirm the board's DONE indicator and use an observable design event: a known LED sequence, UART banner or GPIO transition.

Only after volatile loading is repeatable should persistent configuration be considered. The generic form is:

```sh
openFPGALoader --board nexys_video --write-flash \
  opensource-nexysvideo/nexysvideo.bit
```

Flash programming is slower and survives power cycles; it should be treated as a release operation with a recorded bitstream hash and recovery plan. Consult the board schematic/manual and the installed programmer documentation before selecting a flash target. Keep power and USB connected while flash writing is active.

### Bring-up sequence

Use short feedback loops:

1. Build and archive reports before touching the board.
2. Program SRAM only and check that configuration completes.
3. Verify oscillator/reset health with a simple LED heartbeat.
4. Confirm UART electrical path and baud rate with a boot banner.
5. Confirm the CPU reaches its first known software milestone.
6. Enable external-memory and peripheral tests one at a time.
7. Preserve the successful bitstream, logs, source commit and observations.

The CVW branch maps five user LEDs to bring-up telemetry, including input-clock activity, LiteDRAM initialization state, service-CPU activity and UART activity. This is a sensible replacement for unavailable internal logic-analyzer infrastructure during an open-flow first bring-up; remove or gate diagnostic logic before collecting performance/resource results.

### Timing closure method

When timing fails, begin with the reported endpoints; changing random tool options rarely helps. Determine whether the path is a true synchronous path, a missing clock relationship, a fanout/routing problem, a deep logic cone or a poor architectural boundary. Then make the smallest change that addresses that cause.

| Critical-path pattern | RTL or architecture response |
|---|---|
| Deep arithmetic plus comparison | Pipeline the operation or use a dedicated arithmetic resource |
| Long priority chain | Recode the decision tree, balance selection or register an intermediate result |
| High-fanout control/reset | Reduce fanout, localize enables or use intended distribution resources |
| RAM output into complex decode | Register the RAM output and accept the added cycle explicitly |
| Cross-module ready/valid loop | Break the combinational loop with an elastic register or pipeline stage |
| Slow external interface path | Add valid IO timing constraints and pipeline at the interface if protocol permits |

Retiming may change latency and reset behavior; it is an architectural change unless the interface contract explicitly tolerates it. A RISC-V core cannot arbitrarily insert a cycle into a trap, cache, bus response or forwarding path. Start by preserving observable protocol behavior, then rerun simulation and formal/property checks before relying on the new timing report.

The frequency number emitted by nextpnr should be read as a result under a stated model. It does not include unknown board-level effects, incorrect constraints or unanalysed high-speed domains. A laboratory prototype should aim for margin, particularly when temperature, voltage and USB power conditions differ from the development desktop.

### Multiple clocks and IO timing

Large FPGA systems rarely have a single clock. The Nexys Video Wally example contains the board clock, a generated system clock and DDR-related clocks. Each clock needs a source, frequency, destination registers and a reset relationship. Build a clock table before interpreting STA:

| Clock/domain | Source | Consumers | Required evidence |
|---|---|---|---|
| `clk100` | Board oscillator | Input buffering/clock generation | Pin location, period and clock primitive |
| `HCLK` / system | Generated common clock | Wally, bridge and LiteDRAM bus port | Post-route setup/hold report at target frequency |
| IDELAY/DDR related | DDR PHY clocking | Delay/serializer resources | Correct primitive configuration and explicit timing review |
| JTAG/USB/UART inputs | External asynchronous sources | Debug/serial receiver | Synchronizer or protocol crossing, not ordinary STA |

Declaring clocks asynchronous because a report is inconvenient hides problems. Asynchronous groups are valid only where a real CDC protocol carries data. Generated clocks need an understood parent and ratio, because an unconstrained divided clock makes its paths invisible to analysis. External inputs and outputs require input/output delay assumptions relative to a reference clock when their protocol is synchronous.

### Physical programming diagnostics

If `openFPGALoader` cannot find the cable, first check USB enumeration and permissions, then cable selection and board power. If it loads but DONE never asserts, stop and re-check the part, board target and bitstream hash. If DONE asserts but no behavior appears, test the simplest clock/LED image before investigating Wally software.

| Symptom | First evidence to collect |
|---|---|
| No programmer device | USB cable supports data, board power, user permissions and `--list-cables`/help output |
| Programming error | Exact part/board option, tool version and programming log |
| DONE absent | Bitstream part identity, configuration mode and power/reset state |
| DONE present, no UART | Clock/reset LED, port/baud configuration and firmware image hash |
| Board works once only | Distinguish volatile SRAM from flash configuration and record power-cycle behavior |

Keep USB/JTAG access out of any build script that continuous integration also uses. Building a `.bit` is repeatable in CI, whereas touching a physical board is a separate lab action that someone observes.

## Hands-on Experiments

@sec-complete-case supplies a complementary executed accelerator example using nextpnr's ECP5 backend, a common RTL/configuration manifest and a final placement map. Its 100 MHz target fails at an estimated 86.99 MHz after routing. Inspect its actual timing report and source boundary before comparing it with the board-oriented XC7 workflow here; no Nexys Video or complete-SoC result is implied.

Students without a board follow the alternatives below and the deliverables in [Lab 07](../../labs/07-implementation/README.md#without-a-physical-board). The physical experiments remain available for students with hardware. No experiment requires buying a board to complete the assessed course.

1. [Advanced · C3](../../learning-paths.qmd#sec-path-labels){#act-nextpnr-timing-01 .learning-activity} — Build the Nexys Video configuration and identify the generated JSON, routed JSON, report, FASM, frames and bitstream files.
2. [Advanced · C3](../../learning-paths.qmd#sec-path-labels){#act-nextpnr-timing-02 .learning-activity} — Request 50 MHz instead of 40 MHz without changing RTL. Compare the timing reports and explain why a failing 50 MHz report must not be ignored merely because the 40 MHz configuration runs.
3. [Advanced · C3 · board](../../learning-paths.qmd#sec-path-labels){#act-nextpnr-timing-03 .learning-activity} — Add an LED heartbeat generated from the synchronized system clock. Program SRAM and confirm it after every reset before debugging the processor.
4. [Advanced · C3](../../learning-paths.qmd#sec-path-labels){#act-nextpnr-timing-04 .learning-activity} — Disconnect or rename one XDC port in a copy of the exercise. Observe the implementation error/warning, restore the constraint and verify that the pin name matches the top-level port exactly.
5. [Advanced · C0 · board](../../learning-paths.qmd#sec-path-labels){#act-nextpnr-timing-05 .learning-activity} — Program only SRAM, power-cycle the board and confirm that the configuration vanishes. Then, after following the board-specific procedure, compare this with a deliberately programmed flash image.
6. [Advanced · C0 · board](../../learning-paths.qmd#sec-path-labels){#act-nextpnr-timing-06 .learning-activity} — Create a bring-up record containing commands, board revision, programmer version, UART settings, bitstream hash, DONE state and observed LEDs.

### Alternatives without a board

For experiments 1, 2 and 4, run the implementation tools without connecting hardware: bitstream generation, clock-target comparison and XDC diagnostics are build operations. If tools/databases or compute are unavailable, analyse the instructor-provided baseline/variant reports and failed-constraint example, retaining their source/target/constraint identities. Identify the critical path, margin, unconstrained paths and cause of the failure; propose the next corrective run. Complete your own generic synthesis as well.

For experiment 3, implement a self-checking heartbeat RTL bench with reset assertion/release and a documented simulation divider parameter. Check toggle counts and intervals, preserve a waveform and review logical-port-to-XDC mapping. Restore the intended hardware divider in the synthesis configuration. This is an exercise to implement, not an existing checked heartbeat test.

For experiment 5, submit the expected SRAM/flash power-cycle sequence and explain configuration retention separately from application reset. A digital reset bench cannot establish flash persistence. For experiment 6, produce a bring-up plan with expected DONE/UART/LED observations, recorded build hashes and the first diagnostic action for each missing checkpoint. Mark physical observations as `not_run`; use the real-Wally firmware result from @sec-executable-project for the executable software milestone, identifying its different fixture. Submit the report analysis, waveform/checker, constraint audit and remaining physical tests under the same coursework rubric.

The following chapter applies this complete flow to CORE-V Wally. It identifies what the open Nexys Video configuration implements, how LiteDRAM replaces closed Vivado MIG IP, and which hardware claims are currently supported by evidence.

## Key ideas {#review-nextpnr-timing-ideas .unnumbered .unlisted}

- Placement, routing and timing connect a netlist to a selected FPGA device.
- A bitstream, successful programming and validated board behavior are distinct checkpoints.

## What you should now be able to explain {#review-nextpnr-timing-explain .unnumbered .unlisted}

Explain how constraints and device data affect the physical result, then distinguish temporary JTAG loading from persistent configuration.

## Common mistakes {#review-nextpnr-timing-mistakes .unnumbered .unlisted}

Constraints written for another board or die map pins and clocks to the wrong places, so check them against the part you hold. And generating a bitstream only shows that the tools finished; DDR and peripherals still need their own tests on the board.

## Try it yourself {#review-nextpnr-timing-try .unnumbered .unlisted}

[Advanced · C0](../../learning-paths.qmd#sec-path-labels){#act-nextpnr-timing-review .learning-activity}

Review one existing implementation report against its pin/clock constraints. List the board observations still needed before claiming a working system.
